content: In 2014, the World Health Organization (WHO) released its first set of guidelines aimed at the prevention, care, and treatment of individuals infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV). These guidelines emphasized the assessment of treatment eligibility, initiation of first-line therapies, and monitoring of patients. Currently, WHO is developing new guidelines for testing chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) infections in lowand middle-income settings. One of the key considerations in these guidelines is the potential use of dried blood spots (DBS) for serological and molecular testing of HBV and HCV. This approach could improve access to and uptake of testing in resource-limited settings. To inform these guidelines, a specific research question was developed using the PICOT framework: Among individuals identified for HCV testing, what is the diagnostic accuracy and impact of detecting HCV nucleic acid testing (NAT) using DBS samples compared to venous blood samples? The population of interest included samples for HCV NAT, with the intervention being the use of DBS samples. Comparisons were made with plasma or serum from venous blood samples, and the outcomes assessed included diagnostic accuracy metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio, negative likelihood ratio, true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives. The protocol for this update followed the methodology outlined in the Greenman et al. paper, as published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis. A sensitive search strategy was employed to identify relevant studies in databases such as MEDLINE, CAB abstracts, and Web of Science, covering publications up to August 2013. Only English-language publications were included, and no restrictions were placed on date or geographical location. Abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, and full-text articles were reviewed for eligibility. Additional references were identified through title searches of included articles. Data extraction was performed by two reviewers using predefined categories. Studies were included if they reported on the use of DBS for monitoring and genotyping HCV RNA, including at least one of the following: sensitivity and/or specificity of DBS in HCV RNA viral load quantification, accuracy of DBS for HCV RNA genotyping, or the rate of HCV RNA degradation during transport and storage at room temperature. Nine out of 73 articles met these criteria. For studies measuring HCV RNA presence and quantification, analyses focused on viral load detection endpoints, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) of DBS compared to HCV RNA in plasma. For the question of HCV RNA stability in DBS at room temperature, reviewers extracted data on degradation rates and definitions of room temperature. Studies determining HCV genotype were analyzed for genotype concordance between plasma and DBS, the proportion of HCV RNA-positive DBS samples successfully genotyped, and observed genotypes. The updated review included a search of Medline and PubMed using the same terms as the original systematic review, but with a time limit of 2013 to the present. Statistical analysis was conducted using OpenMeta[Analyst]. Sensitivity and specificity analyses employed bivariate methods with maximum likelihood estimates and 95% confidence intervals. Likelihood ratios were calculated directly from pooled sensitivity and specificity data. Forest plots were used to visually assess heterogeneity. The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias, and a GRADE assessment was performed to evaluate the quality of included studies. The initial review identified 184 titles, of which 17 were selected for full-text review. Nine studies met eligibility criteria, with six reporting outcomes relevant to the PICOT question. In the updated review, 14 articles were identified, and four were selected for full-text review. Two were excluded for not addressing HCV viral load, leaving two studies retained. An additional article identified by an expert was included, resulting in two studies providing sufficient data for meta-analysis. The selected studies were published between 1998 and 2015, with most published between 2007 and 2015. They were conducted in various countries, including the UK, Italy, France, the United States, Lebanon, Brazil, Guinea-Bissau, and Japan. Six studies reported endpoint sensitivity of HCV RNA detection using DBS compared to plasma. Four studies assessed the stability of HCV RNA in DBS at room temperature. Patient characteristics varied across studies, with some focusing on liver clinic attendees, injecting drug users, HIV-infected patients, or general populations. DBS preparation methods also varied, with some studies using capillary blood and others using venous blood. RNA extraction and amplification methods differed across studies. The systematic review and meta-analysis provided evidence of moderate quality supporting the acceptable accuracy of DBS for HCV NAT testing compared to plasma samples. DBS may be a viable option for HCV diagnosis in settings with limited access to venepuncture or inadequate technology for plasma sample preparation and transport. While DBS appears stable under higher temperatures, prolonged storage may lead to viral degradation, potentially affecting quantitative viral load assessments. Further operational research is needed to evaluate DBS accuracy under real-life conditions, including high humidity. Studies using capillary blood for DBS preparation and comparing various commercial test kits and storage conditions would be particularly valuable. Expanded use of HCV NAT testing is critical for improving global HCV diagnosis and treatment. The use of DBS for sample preparation, storage, and transport could enhance the accessibility of this important diagnostic test, particularly in decentralized settings.
